speechtext: The policy to be adopted by the government with respect to unemployment of course has been under consideration constantly. On the orders of the day:

I should like to ask the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gordon) if he has given his final answer to the proposal made by the government of the province of Quebec in connection with the expenditure of $10,000,000 to send young people back to the land, otherwise known as the Vautrin colonization scheme. I saw an announcement in the press the other day in this regard and I should like to ask if the minister has finally concluded not to participate in that scheme.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. A. GORDON (Minister of Immigration and Colonization):
speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
The Vautrin plan was brought to my attention and, through me, to the attention of the government some weeks ago, following the address made by Mr. Vautrin to the convention he called together at Quebec to consider this plan. Of course I am and always have been agreed that there is a very great deal of room for the activities of all those engaged in colonization in connection with our own people here in Canada. I believe I am correct in stating that such colonization is one of the matters coming directly within the ambit of provincial activity, particularly in view of the fact that at the moment, as for some time past, all the lands capable of being used for this purpose belong to the provinces.
The matter was given very great consideration by me, and my views were laid before the government. I do not believe the dominion government should participate in
[Mr. Veniot.l
a colonization plan of this character. Members of the house will remember that assistance was offered and given in a modest way, with no limitation being placed upon the number that could be assisted, but this was not in the nature of a state-aided colonization plan; rather it was a plan that we hoped would appeal to the provinces and the municipalities. To a considerable measure it did appeal to them and was taken advantage of by them. If my recollection serves me right the agreements with the provinces, with the exception of Prince Edward Island, are still in force and the plan outlined was in fact entirely in the nature of a plan to relieve unemployment to the extent that it would place people on the land; it was a relief plan pure and simple. It may be that time will disclose the desirability of the dominion government assisting provincial colonization plans, but at the moment the decision of the government is that assistance will not be given to such a plan as the Vautrin scheme.

speechtext:
On February 26, Mr. Pouliot asked if the government proposed to proceed with a bill based on a convention which lapsed fourteen years ago.
This argument is based on the wording of article 19 of the convention, which provides that each member which ratifies this convention agrees to bring	its provisions
into operation not later than July 1, 1921. Such articles fixing a maximum time limit for the bringing into operation of the provisions of conventions, were inserted in conventions adopted prior to 1928 in order to facilitate their entry into force for different countries at the same time. States members of the international labour organization are, of course, free to ratify conventions at their own time, and, moreover, they clearly cannot be obliged to bring a convention into operation before they have ratified it. In conventions adopted since 1928 no such article purporting to fix a maximum time limit appears. The article in question has no application to members ratifying after the named date, and such members are bound by the convention from the date of the registration of their ratification in accordance with the provisions of article 18. In support of this view two facts may be cited:
(a)	The constant practice of the members of the organization, many of whom have ratified conventions after the named dates and have been considered as bound from the date of registration of the ratification;
(b)	The view taken of the article in question by the international labour conference in 1928 when it was agreed to suppress it as superfluous in future conventions. In 1927 Mr. Morellet, the legal adviser of the international labour office gave it as his opinion that the legal force of articles such as article 19 of the hours of work convention was as follows:
When a state ratifies after the date fixed by the clause, the clause has no effect for that state; when, on the contrary, a state ratifies before this date, it has the benefit of a waiting period and may abstain from applying the convention until the date fixed.
It might be pointed out that nineteen countries have ratified the convention limiting hours of work since July 1, 1921, the date cited in the article on which Mr. Pouliot bases his case that the convention has lapsed.

subtopic: BILL TO LIMIT HOURS OP WORK IN INDUSTRIAL UNDERTAKINGS
speechtext: The workers employed in restaurants and hotels are not included in this bill. I believe that if the government investigated the conditions in this occupation they would probably find that the hours of labour are longer and the conditions more intolerable than in any industrial establishment in Canada, and I see no reason why these men and women should not be included in the provisions of this bill. Quite recently I went into a restaurant in this city and asked a man how many hours a day he worked and he said he worked 365 days a year and ten hours a day, from eight at night until five o'clock in the morning. If it is essential that there should be an eight hour working day in the industrial structure of the country, I think it is just as essential, and just as practical, for the government to provide that these same conditions surrounding the hours of labour should be enforced in the restaurants and hotels of the country. A large number of workers are involved, and the enforcement of legislation such as this in all these establishments would be comparatively simple; indeed, it would be far more simple in my opinion than the enforcement of the law in some of the outlying districts where this legislation will govern those employed in mines, quarries and industrial establishments. I would ask the Minister of Labour why the government leaves outside the jurisdiction of this legislation so large a body of workers, who in my opinion are vitally in need of legislative action to curtail the intolerably long hours and to improve the conditions that exist in many sections of this particular calling in Canada.

We can all sympathize with the class of workers to whom the hon. member has referred. This legislation however is based upon the convention which was ratified by this parliament and which interprets "industrial undertakings." The bill follows the convention very closely; in fact, throughout it follows the wording of the convention itself. Moreover, it must be remembered that the provinces have legislation which covers the very
point the hon. member has raised, and the process provided by the various provincial statutes can be resorted to. It may be that the future will disclose some method whereby this parliament can assist the provinces in working out plans to relieve these workers, who perhaps do not come within the scope of the convention and of this bill. But inasmuch as the bill follows the convention, I am afraid that at present the workers referred to by the hon. gentleman will have to resort to provincial legislation, which covers their situation.

subtopic: BILL TO LIMIT HOURS OP WORK IN INDUSTRIAL UNDERTAKINGS
speechtext: The legislation in Ontario governing this class of workers is not worth the paper it is written on. While I am aware that this bill is based on the convention of the international labour office, I would point out that the convention lays down only a minimum; there is no regulation, there is no law, there is no advice to any government as to how far it shall go beyond the minimum fixed by the convention. If I am not mistaken, the hours of labour permitted under the factories act of Ontario are limited to sixty a week. I could understand the minister's position if this were a peculiar industry where regulations would be difficult or the enforcement of the law would present obstacles, but I see no reason why the men and women engaged in this particular calling should not come within the jurisdiction of this act, because the women and girls are more or less defenceless. Indeed, that might be said of the occupation generally. I suppose it is fair to say that the wages paid in the catering business are among the lowest in the dominion. Before this section is passed I think the minister should take into serious consideration the suggestion I have made. I think it would be well to let the section stand until the government can come to a decision to include the men and women engaged in this industry, from one end of Canada to the other, within the provisions of this bill, so that they may have the benefit of the eight hour day.

speechtext:
I would like to ask the minister whether he has considered the question of the effect of the supreme court decision as reported in 47 Supreme Court Reports at page 505 in regard to hours of labour. I do not propose to argue the matter, because it has been referred to before and will be dealt with later, but before the clause passes I would like to direct the minister's attention to that decision which is one bearing directly on this question, and it is clearly to this effect:
That the matter of labour in industrial undertakings in Canada, is primarily within the competence of provincial legislatures, but parliament can legislate as to labour in territories not yet organized into, or forming part of, a province and as to labour of servants of the dominion if these are within the scope of the draft convention.
I just wanted to call the minister's attention to the fact that this decision is not referred to in either the radio decision or the aeronautics decision which were relied upon by the Prime Minister as possibly giving jurisdiction. So far it has not been referred to, distinguished or overruled, and of course I take it that it stands. I do not propose to argue the matter at any length, but I wanted to know whether the minister had considered it. Surely this decision, as it stands, makes this legislation entirely ultra vires.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
subtopic: BILL TO LIMIT HOURS OP WORK IN INDUSTRIAL UNDERTAKINGS
speechtext:
Of course I am not unacquainted with the decision to which the hon. member has made reference. We have either
Eight Hour Day

heard in this chamber or read very able arguments made in another place in this parliament by a number of lawyer members of both chambers. I was very much interested in hearing the argument of the Prime Minister, and the very clear and lucid argument of the hon. member for Quebec East, and in reading in the minutes of the Senate the arguments of those who so clearly spread upon the record their views as to whether this legislation is intra or ultra vires this parliament. I do not know that I can add anything to what has been said by those gentlemen. I think perhaps it would do us good as lawyers to read with care the arguments that were advanced. There are many nimble minded men in the legal profession and some I presume in other professions, as well as profound philosophers who have spoken and WTitten about questions of this character. This parliament has, with perhaps some reservations, agreed to the principle which underlies this legislation. I believe that hon. members of this chamber are profoundly concerned, not so much with those arguments, lucid as some of them were, and obscure as were others, with respect to the constitutionality of the measure, but about the great majority of the people of this country who desire the passage of this legislation and who I think we all believe will be very greatly benefited by it and by its proper administration. Therefore while the hon. member for West Middlesex has raised the question of this decision of our supreme *court, I can only repeat that I have listened to and read the very illuminating arguments on this point that have taken place in this chamber and in another place during recent weeks. I can add nothing to or subtract nothing from them, I think they have covered the ground pretty well.

I asked the minister a question a few minutes ago as to having some uniformity with provincial legislation as far as exceptions and exemptions were concerned. The question I now ask is consequent on that. Take for example an industry in British Columbia, some 3,000 miles from the minister's office in Ottawa; does he contemplate having provincial machinery there which can be appealed to in a moment in case of an industrial accident where an exception specified in provincial legislation can be resorted to, or what does he contemplate to meet an emergency situation of that kind?

Section 10 of this bill reads:
10. (1) The governor in council may also make regulations permitting - f.Mr. Gordon.]
(a) permanent exceptions to the limits of hours of work fixed by this act in ease of preparatory or complementary work which must necessarily be carried on outside the limits laid down for the general working of an establishment, or for certain classes of workers whose work is essentially intermittent;
Then of course section 7 covers other exceptional cases. I had hoped that we would take the sections up seriatim, but -since we have not adopted that course I will try to deal with points as they arise. I have given that section a great deal of thought, having regard to just such situations as referred to by the hon. member. I know of cases in various parts of Canada which it would perhaps be extremely difficult if not impossible to bring exactly within the four corners of the bill. When section 10 is under discussion I was going to ask that it stand and perhaps by that time I may have an amendment to suggest, if there is doubt here-and there may be-as to whether or not subsection 1 (a) of section 10 goes far enough to exempt from the operation of the bill some of those undertakings which in the very nature of things would have most difficulty in complying with the requirement of an eight hour day. The danger of course always is that a bill which is reformatory in its character and, we all hope, remedial in the best sense of the word, by providing for exemptions might itself be imperilled or destroyed. That situation must be avoided. I think perhaps section 10 might be amended, placing in the governor in council some further or more defim'te authority, so that these exceptional cases can be dealt with by regulations which, at any rate until they are shown to be insufficient, will be permanent in their nature, and can be subject to prompt revision to suit conditions or emergences which might arise, particularly in avocations such as the hon. member for Vancouver Centre suggested. These occur mainly in the northern parts of Canada and are not referable so much to the highly industrialized centres. I will speak to this point again when section 10 is under discussion

One
further observation, because this is very important to us in the far west. Section 10 (b) refers to temporary exemptions. My point is mainly with respect to the machinery which the department would use in making immediate decisions as to possible temporary exceptions made necessary either by accident or by other causes referred to in the provincial statutes. provinces, or would they have inspectors in the various provinces with authority to make immediate decisions with regard to these temporary exceptions?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: I believe that the industries that might be seriously affected can be sufficiently identified and are sufficiently well known that all these conditions can be taken care of in the regulations. The regulations of course would be subject to revision from time to time. I can well understand that legislation of this character to be effective must be progressive in its nature. It has to be understood and administered in such a way that industry will not be impeded, and those for whom the legislation was specially passed will not have their position imperilled. There will have to be a great deal of thought given to the regulations, and when we come to section 10 I may suggest that the powers of the governor in council be made more clear with respect to framing regulations applying them to industrial conditions such as those to which the hon. member for Vancouver Centre and others have referred.

In doing that it must
not be forgotten that this act can be regulated out of existence.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: I stated that.

I do not like to see
those powers there. Take the Lord's Day Act, it was considered a great thing, but the ink was hardly dry on it until, in my judgment, it wTas made useless by regulations. This act can be regulated out of existence. I have had some experience in connection with the reduction of the hours of labour, and I do not know of any case where long hours are worked to-day in which they could not put up the best argument in the world why such hours must continue. It will take some ingenuity on the part of employers to meet legislation of this description. They will have to sit down and think their way through. The act will not be worth much if the governor in council has the power to except so many people from its provisions by regulation. And what is more important is that the people who frame the regulations shall be sympathetic to the purpose of the act. I believe that in the next ten years we shall go a long way further than the provisions of this act; this merely lays the foundation stone. If we can jump the legal hurdles that have been put up by some people on this side of the house, in my judgment it will be the greatest contribution
made by this parliament in connection with social legislation, and I hope the government is successful, and that those on this side will be able to follow in their wake if they are the next government.

I would like
to say just a word by way of correction of what my hon. friend has said. He has spoken about political hurdles which he says have been put up by this side. This side has put up no hurdles whatever. Attention has been drawn by this side to what appear to be hurdles actually in existence, but that is a very different thing from being responsible for putting them up.

I did not mean political hurdles, I said legal hurdles. I am not questioning for a moment the sincerity of the men who have come to certain conclusions. But in my judgment, taking a long view of the thing, it is absolutely essential that we should take national action on these very vital questions, if democratic institutions are to be preserved. If we think we can carry on indefinitely in this country with a million and a half people on relief, and place obstacles of a constitutional character in their way, we are just fooling ourselves, that is all. I believe that sincerely; I am just as sincere in that statement as those hon. members who take the position that this measure is what the lawyers call ultra vires. I am not one given to extravagant expressions of opinion, either in this house or back in my own city.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: Some call it intra vires.

Some call it that, but
whether it is ultra vires or intra vires, I think we should press it to a conclusion.

Speaking about fooling one's self, I submit it may be only fooling one's self to assume that this parliament has power to do things which the courts may hold it has not power to do. In pointing out that the last word in the question of ultra vires or intra vires is going to be given by the courts, no one is seeking to block any legislation; we are rather seeking to hasten the day when what may be an obstacle will be removed and the proper method of procedure adopted.

The only way to hasten
the day when the obstacles in the way will be removed is to keep hammering away at the legislation, and very little along that line has been done federally. We have a good deal of social legislation on the statute books of the various provinces; we also have
Eight Hour Day

dominion legislation of that kind, but all this legislation is largely a dead letter because the employees engaged in the particular industries dare not draw the attention of the authorities to infractions of these laws. I think that has been brought out quite clearly in the investigation that has been going on here in the last year.
I do not think the people for whom the hon. member for Vancouver Centre was speaking need feel concerned about the rigidity of the act. I feel that it will have to be very rigid and definite, but that does not mean that in its operation that rigidity will be continued. If the employers concerned have proper regard for their employees, with proper understandings and agreements, I think, there will be no difficulty in getting the employees to carry on in any emergency. I speak with some knowledge; I have been engaged in industry and have to had to do with employers. I know that where employees are decently treated and consulted by their employers there is no difficulty at all in getting such employees to carry on in an emergency. There is scarcely a law on our statute books which would not defeat itself if it were administered according to the terms and letter of the statute. That cannot be done. I have in mind particular regulations in regard to street car service in the city of Vancouver, and I presume the same situation prevailed in other cities. I remember that the legislature passed very drastic regulations in regard to the operation of the street cars in Vancouver. We drew the attention of the management to the fact that the street car service could not be operated if all the regulations were carried out, and we had a letter from the attorney general of the province telling us to carry on as we always had done.
The point I wish to make now is that if this law is to be enforced-I have not in mind now the question of whether or not it is ultra vires-it can have application only in those industries where the workers are well organized. In that regard I might say that if the government wish to see the legislation bring forth fruit they should promote organization among the employees of industry in this country. I agree with the hon. member for East Hamilton ; I have no fear that the law may become too rigid. We are all reasonable people where our living is concerned, and those engaged in industry certainly are not going to advocate the sabotage of industry if it is carried on by the employers in a reasonable manner, and if the employers do not attempt to take advantage of openings that the legislation may give them.

Before this section is
carried I want to refer once more to the hotel and restaurant employees. I think they should come under the provisions of this act. I do not want to go over all the ground I covered a few moments ago, and I am fully aware that the minister does not care to make a snap judgment on the matter, but the reason he has given as to why these employees are not under this legislation is not satisfactory to me. Through you, Mr. Chairman, I would ask the minister to let this section stand, to study the matter for twenty-four hours and see whether it is not possible to include this large army of workers who, perhaps more than the organized labour movement, need the advantage of legislation of this description. We know that the average girl goes to work as a stepping stone to getting married, for better or worse, and it is hard to organize them. It is only natural that many employers should take advantage of this fact, and that statement applies to the industry in general. In normal times it is an industry in which the labour turn-over is very high; men go into and out of it as a matter of course, and in my

judgment it would be a really constructive measure if the government could see its way clear to include these employees under this act. So I would ask the minister to let the section stand for twenty-four hours in order that he might go into the matter.

I want to
endorse that suggestion. I do not need to stress it further; I believe the minister is just as sympathetic as we are, and he knows that the employment of young people-and there are large numbers of very young people employed in restaurants and hotels-for these long hours is detrimental to their general health. It is not a happy condition for the country, and now that we are applying a general eight hour law surely we should make that law apply to hotel and restaurant services. I do not see why those people should be exempted; there is no good reason for it. The fact that they do not come withip the socalled interpretation of the labour conventions does not prevent the government providing that paragraph (b) of section 2 should include these employees. They alter, clean, do ornamental work, adapt for consumption, transform materials for use, and so on. I would like the minister to consider this matter carefully.

I do not think there can be any possible doubt as to the advantage of an eight hour day; as a matter of fact we have had the eight hour day in most industries for some considerable time. In my life time there has been a very great change. I remember that in my boyhood days shipyard work demanded a twelve hour day, and that situation existed in many other industries as well. The length of the working day has a very important effect on the accidents in industry; as to that there is no possible doubt. There are three periods during which accidents reach their highest point. The first is Monday morning, or the morning after a holiday; that is the hour in which most accidents occur. The next is the first hour or hour and a half of the ordinary working day, or from seven o'clock to eight o'clock or half past eight, and the third accident period is the closing hour in the afternoon. If hon. members will give the matter a little thought they will realize that I have stated the facts. Some few men who go off on a week-end holiday, or for a holiday longer than that, perhaps do not spend their time in the best possible manner, with the result that Monday mornings following holidays produced their crop of accidents. Of course I speak about the steel works, machine shop work and work
Eight Hour Day
in the rolling mills and forges. There we had first aid equipment, a registered nurse in attendance and an ambulance service always available.
There are other phases of the matter which I believe should be given the attention of hon. members. I do not know whether or not I am in order when I attempt to take them up at this time. There are several classes of workers who could not come under the operation of eight-hour day legislation; certainly fishermen and farmers could not. The farmer's day is never done, at least in certain seasons of the year. We could not control his working hours; no legislation enacted by this parliament or any legislative body could do that.
Then we come to that type of operations in which materials are transformed. Let us for a moment consider blast furnaces. A blast furnace operation is continuous from the time the furnace is blown in until it is blown out. That period of time may be one year, it may be five years, nine years or even longer than that. The fact is that so long as the furnace is in blast the operation is continuous; it operates on Sunday, Monday and every other day and no regard is had for the end of the week, holidays or any regulations which may be made.
Mr. MITOHElLL:	The eight hour day is
used in blast furnace operations, both in the United States and in 'Canada.

No. To a large extent
the same observations would apply to open hearth furnaces, because those furnaces take the hot metal from the blast furnaces. These are factors which have to be considered, and I assume before we have completed consideration of the bill they will have been given due consideration.
Reverting to the case of blast furnaces, the large blowing engines furnishing the blast to the furnaces are entirely automatic and are housed in buildings well lighted, with tiled floors and kept scrupulously clean, bright and comfortable. The engines are practically completely self-controlled. While the usual working pressure of the blast furnace is about 10 pounds per square inch in the event of a hang-up in the furnace stack, the resistance may become so great as to run the pressure up to 30, 40 or even 50 pounds per square inch. On the other hand, when the furnace is being tapped and the molten metal drawn off, the wind is practically shut off and these big engines then idle along, revolving very slowly. The engineers who attend them are white-collared men with practically nothing to do except
Eight Hour Day

when trouble develops. They customarily and, in fact, invariably work twelve hour shifts and have been vehemently opposed to an eight hour shift in so far as they are concerned.
It sounds nice.

Those are the factors
which have to be considered. I have no doubt that before we have completed consideration of the bill we may make some alterations to provide for circumstances such as I have indicated, and others which I have in mind but shall not refer to at the present time.

A few moments ago the
minister said that the passage of this legislation would work to the great advantage of the majority of workers. So far as that is concerned I agree with him, but I am wondering if he has considered the conditions which obtain in some localities. I believe this legislation will help large numbers of workers in urban centres where great numbers are out of employment during some seasons of the year, and where there are more wmrkers available than are now required or have for some time been required by the. industries. However conditions are different in other parts of the country.
I live in a part of Canada where there are a limited number of small industries connected with lumbering. I refer to sawmills, wood processing mills, and planing mills. This work is seasonable, there being work for only a certain number of months in the year. Sawmills can be operated only a certain number of months because the lumber has to be sawn early in the season and piled for purposes of drying. In the last two weeks, following the presentation of the bill I have been approached by workmen connected with these lumbering operations, and they have told me that the adoption of an eight hour day regulation during the summer season would not be in their interests. They suggest the minister should consider the matter of leaving optional with the workers any arrangements which may be made between employers and employees towards a ten hour day, or sixty hour week. They suggest further however that it should be left to them to state whether or not the eight hour day would be accepted.
There is a further consideration which I should like to bring to the attention of the minister. In the constituency from which I come a limited number have work during the busy season, and during that time they collect savings to carry them through the winter season.	During the winter season
their working	hours are	very greatly

decreased. The present legislation would bind them to work only eight hours a day or forty-eight hours a w^eek in the best season of the year, and I am wondering how they would collect their savings to carry them through the season when work is scarce. During that time they may be unemployed or be employed only fifty per cent of the time. When we reach sections 9 and 10 the minister may feel inclined to redraft the legislation so that arrangements between employers and employees may be optional, and thereby permit a sixty hour week during certain months of the year.

I have been interested i;n the observations of the hon. member for Pietou. So far as I am concerned it is my belief that the twenty-four hour operation is about the simplest with which we have to deal. If two shifts are required to conduct a twenty-four hour operation, then three shifts of eight hours would do the work just as well. In that event however the workers would expect a higher rate per hour so that their wages might be favourably comparable with those they earned on the longer shifts. Therein lies the danger, so far as business is concerned. This change would undoubtedly increase production costs. Provided customs tariffs are maintained at a high level such an arrangement might not hurt us in our own country, but undoubtedly our export trade would be affected.
Representations have been made to me from various sources, and particularly from the smaller communities, and I believe it would be well for the minister to consider what I have said, should he choose to redraft section 10. Then, may I ask him this question : How many countries have adopted the eight hour day convention?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
The difficulties raised by the hon. member have been in my mind, and I realize further, that if th:s law is to prevail there must be a very considerable readjustment in industrial undertakings. In my view it will never operate successfully unless all parties interested, and the government seeking to enforce the measure, deal with the matter with the utmost frankness and unselfishness. If the employers and employees exhibit an attitude of self preservation, with some degree of selfishness, and if the government has no method of control then in attempting to pass the legislation we are wasting our time.
When legislation of this kind is introduced for the first time there are bound to be circumstances which are not covered, but I believe we are acting quite properly if we

make a beginning with the confidence that our constitutional position is sound. We do not wish to have the legislation take in too wide a circle only to be confronted with confusion, and the great difficulty of narrowing the circle to where it should have been in the beginning. I hope I shall live to see the day when legislation of this kind will be widened to include every worker in this country, but one of the things we must remember is that when we are embarking on such legislation we had better be sure of the ground we are on to-day, gradually enlarging the circle to take in other vocations and activities, rather than in the words of the street biting off more than we can chew.
Will this act apply to saw mills, logging camps and fish plants?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: Yes.
To fish plants? I thought the hon. member-

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: Unless there is an exception.

I thought the hon. member for Gloucester pointed out that it would be difficult to rim a fish plant unless they were exempted, because the fish had to be treated as they came in. I have received representations from British Columbia to the effect that it will be very difficult to run fish plants on the basis here proposed. A plant may be idle for a week waiting for fish to come along, and then they come in in large quantities and the men work until the fish have all been treated. I have in mind pilchards from which oil and meal are made. Sometimes the fish do not come in for a day or a week, and then they are brought in in large quantities. And the same in the handling of salmon for canning purposes. As regards the particular company that got into communication with me, I drew their attention to section 2, pointing out that I did not think it would apply to fish plants. If however, the minister assures me now that this provision will apply to these plants then the situation is indeed a serious one, because the fish must be handled when they are fresh, and men who have been idle for a day or two are willing to work extra. It would be disastrous to the salmon and pilchard industries of British Columbia if any other interpretation than that should prevail. Paragraph (b) includes industries in which articles are manufactured, altered, cleaned, repaired, ornamented, finished and so forth. Well, pilchards are not altered, though they are cleaned; nor are they repaired or ornamented, but they might be said to be manufactured. If the minister's statement is
Eight Hour Day
given after full consideration of the subject, then I suggest that the section should stand. The government should consider the disastrous effects which the section as it is now is likely to have in British Columbia.

Who asked for this legislation? Have the people engaged in industry asked that this eight hour day be put into effect? Has organized labour asked for it? This is an important measure which affects the lives of all the workers in Canada and of everyone else, whether producer, manufacturer or consumer. In my opinion this legislation is absolutely unworkable. As a matter of fact, employers of labour in this country have got together in the last fifteen years with the result that we have now an eight hour day wherever it is possible. In my business the men work sometimes fifteen and twenty hours and on other days tney work only two or three hours, but the men are delighted to get fifteen or twenty hours of work because we pay them time and a half over eight hours. Where the employment is steady, men work only from eight o'clock until five. When I am having my breakfast I can hear the whistles blowing at eight o'clock, and if my window is open, I can hear them again Mowing for the knock-off hour at five o'clock. We do not need this legislation. Who demanded it? Is this part of the reform program? If it is it is a pretty cheap method of trying to influence a cert-aiin number of votes in the country at the expense of the people. I know, from the way the minister spoke, that he is not sincere about this legislation; he knows it is not right and cannot work out. Why should one class work eight hours a day and others ten, fifteen and twenty hours if necessary? If you could pass legislation that would deal with everyone on the same basis, chen I would say, put it on the statute books; but until you can do that, then I say there should be no discrimination. Take the unemployment insurance legislation: why should certain classes come under the provisions of that act while others who have to contribute will not derive any benefit from it? The same applies to this so-called legislation; it is a snare and a delusion, and the minister and his colleagues sitting in the front benches, including the minister from Pictou, know that what 1 am saying is correct. We are trying to get this country out of the hole and we are willing to spend our money to give the people work whenever possible, but this legislation will put back the hands of the clock. It is not necessary, because for years we have
Eight Hour Day

had a forty-eight hour week and an eight hour day, and it is only in cases of necessity that men have worked overtime, and they have got paid for it. I can understand that in the old days the situation was different when people were paid by the day, irrespective of the number of hours they worked. They worked ten or twelve hours and got paid by the day or the month. But to-day men are paid by the hour and for overtime they get time and a half or even double time. I have paid my men on that basis and I am delighted to do so-and I work as hard as they do and often do not get very much out of it. I say, let us get out of the hole first. If we ca.n pass a national law to cover everyone, I am for that law; but I do not believe in stepbairns in the family. Everyone should be treated alike. I know the minister realizes that this legislation will never be effective, and he should move that the committee rise and report progress and let this bill go t,o the foot of the order paper, not to be brought up until after the election.

I hope the minister will make a statement in reply to the representations I have made in connection with fish plants. If what he has already said represents his attitude I must put on record a telegram I received on February 22, from one of the largest fish plants in British Columbia. This telegram reads:
Just had opportunity of reading details proposed eight hour day draft convention. Although, in principle, consider eight hour day sound, feel, very strongly, that this company must be exempted' therefrom because fishing, fish canning and processing are definitely seasonal and it is utterly impossible to restrict daily or weekly supplies, during season, to ensure performance under requirements of said draft convention since, owing to perishable nature of the commodity, same must be eared for and processed immediately after delivery.
There is no means of telling what each day or week will bring; each plant must be in position to care for what fish is tendered as tendered; consequently, although every effort has been made in the past and will continue to be made in the future to restrict hours of labour, it is a physical impossibility for this company to assume the conditions set forth in the draft convention.
The provincial government, in administering the eight hour day legislation, recognizes position of this industry and grant the necessary exemption.
Furthermore, in our markets, which are largely export, competition is already sufficiently keen and subject to sufficient handicap without still further hampering by rigid eight hour day requirements.
Shall, therefore, much appreciate your assurance that exemption requested be granted.
At that time the company had not seen the actual bill but only the convention. I im-

mediately mailed them a copy of the bill and said that, so far as I could judge, the definition of industrial undertaking in section 2, while somewhat vague, would appear to leave the fishing industry out of the operation of the bill, and that seemed to me to be not only necessary but reasonable. I received a letter from the company in which the writer said that he had looked at the definition given in section 2 and that it seemed to indicate that the industry would not come within the operations of the bill. It was only intense Scotch caution that led me to ask definitely for a statement from the minister to the effect that it did not apply. The hon. member for Gloucester raised the question in connection with the sardine industry and was told, I thought, that the industry would not come under the bill. It would be disastrous if this provision were held to apply to these fish processing and canning plants. The minister., unwittingly, is not playing fair to the industry when he couches the provision in such ambiguous language, because I thought it was all right and the company in Vancouver-and they have Lawyers there -were also under the impression that the industry was exempt. Now the minister says it will not be exempt, and I cannot protest too strongly. At least he should allow the section to stand until the interests in British Columbia are given an opportunity to make representations, because their belief is that they do not come under the bill.

It has always been the lot of labour to have to fight the employer. I remember when as a boy I saw men working twelve and fourteen hours in the steel mills. The employers of that day said to the labourers, "If you get ten hours a day we shall have to shut down our plants." They were given a ten hour day and later when a plea was made for an eight hour day the same excuse was given-it would ruin industry and cost more. I think this measure should meet with support from every section of the house. It is a step in the right direction. Personally, I am all for this measure, but the reason I rise is just to point out to the committee that if there is a twenty-four hour day operation and a continuous operation in those mills for three hundred and sixty-five days in the year, it is the easiest thing in the world to put on three shifts. I am strongly of opinion -and I say this from a labour point of view- if labour had stressed shorter hours instead of higher wages, I believe labour to-day would be in a better position because employers have to provide food, shelter and clothing for

Eight Hour Day
those labourers. The reason I rise is to support the bill, and I wish to see it go on to the statute books so that all in the dominion will come under its provisions.

I agree with the hon. member for New Westminster that a big manufacturing company can put on different shifts, but how is this going to apply to small plants?
I am thinking in my town of some foundries and mills that are just able to exist and employ five or six hands who are sometimes working ten hours a day. It is going to be a hardship for these organizations to be limited to eight hours a day. I am thinking of a big milling company in a city in my constituency. It has ceased to operate; a man has leased the small mill there and he is operating it ten hours a day. He employs five men; be has never cut those men's wages, and they are well satisfied and want to continue working as they are doing. Would their hours of work have to be reduced to eight?
In regard to restaurants we have in our city a good couple, white people, who are conducting a first class restaurant and who are employing all white labour. I was given some figures just last Saturday night in regard to this. They are paying out over $8,000 in wages a year and this money is all spent in our city; it is not sent away to any foreign country. They pay S150 a month rent for the premises they occupy; their power runs them $100 a month, and their business taxes come to about $115 a year. They have a baker's licence and also a restaurant licence. Their girls work only fifty hours a week, but their boys are working longer hours. These were boys who were working on a farm-

How .many hours a
week are the boys working?

Those boys have a position
there at $9 a week. They get their board and room. They are working longer than eight hours a day, but it would be a hardship on those people to enforce an eight hour day because it would drive the business to restaurants run by foreigners. I would like to know how one would keep track of how many hours a Chinese is working. When it is hard for companies to exist, I think it is a poor time to introduce an eight hour day. If all factories were busy and everybody had a position, the plan proposed would be much more workable. As I see the situation, I am not in favour of this legislation at all.

I have heard arguments of this kind all my life, and I think we should get down to earth. If long hours and low
wages are the measure of civilization of any country, India and China would be the most prosperous in the world. Let us be frank about the matter. I have heard it said here several times this afternoon:	There will be
a great deal of difficulty; it will be a hardship to change from these long hours for $9 a week like those the hon. member has just been discussing. The hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough said that he had the eight hour day among his employees. This bill is not intended to deal with the fair employer; it is intended to deal with the unfair employer who will not cooperate, who will take advantage of the good employer and work his men an extra couple of hours a day so as to get the advantage under those conditions.

What if they get paid by
the hour?

Some do and some do not. Everybody in this country is not paid by the hour. Frankly, I do not think the bill goes far enough. I have before me a copy of World Current History which points out that a six hour day was introduced in Italy this year.
That was enforced whether they liked it or not.

I know that was done
under a dictatorship in Italy. This is being done under a democracy in this country. I know there are many who will be opposed to a shorter day, and anybody who has experience with certain men knows that is always the case, but a start has to be made somewhere. This bill should be more comprehensive, and I agree with the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough in that regard. There is an important industry, that of distribution, which was discussed in the price spreads committee; I refer to the chain stores, and it is more important for them to come within the confines of the bill than it is for anybody else. The federal government or the provincial governments, whichever win out on the legal aspect of the matter, are going to go a long way further than this legislation if they are to meet the needs of the masses not only in industry but in agriculture. Let us take the case of the United States. If they got back to the production capacity of 1929, there would still be 6,000,000 people out of work in that country. The question that is confronting the people not only of Canada but of the United States is:	What are we
going to do about the matter? The workmen in their practical way know that the only real advance they have ever made has been in
Eight Hour Day

shortening the working day. In Italy by reducing in certain industries the working hours from eight to six they have been able to put 130,000 more people at work. In Canada, if the leadership is not going to come from this House of Commons, I do not know where it will come from. If this house is not going to say to those unfair employers, those employers who take advantage of the good ones, that certain things must be done, I do not know of any other agency that can deal with the matter. The last thing in the world for a member of this house to do is to argue in favour of anybody who would take boys off the farm and make them work twelve hours a day for 89 a week. Let us not shed tears over any such employer. Those are the conditions we have heard brought out in the price spread investigation. This legislation will apply to the Chinese or the Greeks just the same as to the native born Canadian. The intent of it is to see that everybody gets a fair deal, because everybody is equal in the eyes of the law. I do not think it becomes any member to shed tears about a man who works a boy in a restaurant twelve hours a day for S9 a week. That instance used shows all the more reason why we should have legislation of this description.

When I referred a few minutes ago to the difficulties of the situation and said that some regulations would have to be made in that connection, I hope the committee did not form the opinion that I was opposed to an eight hour day, because I am not. For more than twenty years our practice was to have a sixty hour week; to-day I believe a forty-four hour week will produce more in the course of a year and under better conditions for both the workmen and the employer than would a longer week. If the committee will bear with me, I shall give one or two reasons why I hold that opinion. In a steel plant the repair gang is an important part of the organization. Under ordinary conditions twenty years ago when the mills ceased work at six o'clock Saturday night, the repair gang of thirty or forty men came cn, worked all Saturday night, all day Sunday and all Sunday night to get the mills, hammers, presses and furnaces into proper condition for resuming work on Monday morning. About twenty years ago some men came into my office one Saturday and suggested that Saturday afternoon during the summer months from June to September should be a holiday. I thought the idea was a good one and agreed to it. What was the result? We were able to get our repair work all completed in the Saturday afternoon and

Saturday night or by Sunday morning without any Sunday work, which the repair gang appreciated. That also meant a considerable saving so far as the cost of repairs was concerned because Sunday work was paid double time. All needed repairs were completed, whereas under former conditions there very often was not time enough between six o'clock Saturday night and Monday morning to complete the repairs. At the end of that season I decided that a half holiday on Saturday was the proper thing every month in the year, and it has been in effect ever since. To-day more goods can be produced in a forty-four hour week in almost every line of manufacture than in sixty or seventy hours twenty years ago; I think we all agree as to that. The hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough thinks this legislation is not required. It is required in some sections of the country at least in regard to some operations. There will have to be a good deal done by way of providing for the classes of labour that I referred to a little while ago, and it will be only by trial and error and changes and modifications in the next two or three years to get it working smoothly that we shall finally get the measure in such shape that practically everyone will be in favour of it.

I am sure that most if not all hon. members are in sympathy with the suggestion which has been made by the hon. member for East Hamilton. But I understand that this bill is drafted for the purpose of implementing an undertaking given by Canada in connection with draft conventions approved by the international labour office at Geneva. I understand that the bill on that account conforms in essence with the draft convention. My hon. friend from East Hamilton says: "But why should not this parliament go beyond the minimum requirements of the draft convention and enact a measure which will include more classes and perhaps go even further in respect to the limitation of hours?" I suggest this to him and to the committee: I understand that one of the grounds on which parliament bases its jurisdiction to pass a measure of this kind is that it is an attempt to implement a treaty agreement, and if it were not, whatever ground or basis of jurisdiction we have would be to that extent weakened. For that reason I suggest that the moment we go beyond that ground we are weakening our position in respect of jurisdiction, and that only by keeping within the limits of our treaty obligations are we safe in respect of our right to pass the legislation, so far as such obligations are a ground of our jurisdiction.

Eight Hour Day

Will the hon. gentleman state, as clearly as he is now stating his case to the committee, in what respect the draft convention-which by the way was not a labour convention from Geneva but comes under the treaty of Versailles- limits the power of this government to include such categories as restaurant and hotel work?

My answer is that as I understand the situation, one of the grounds of our jurisdiction to pass this legislation is the fact that as a nation we have undertaken to pass legislation of this kind. That, as I understand it, gives to this parliament a jurisdiction which it might not otherwise have. My suggestion is that if that be so, the scope of our jurisdiction will be limited to the scope of our obligations derived from such undertaking. In other words if our jurisdiction depends upon or is derived from our obligation, to that extent, in order to keep within our jurisdiction so derived, we must keep within our obligation.
But will the hon. gentleman show me how we are limited? What is the obligation? Wild he read the part that refers to that?

Here is the preamble to the bill:
Whereas the Dominion of Canada is a signatory, as part of the British empire, to the treaty of peace made between the allied and associated powers and Germany, signed at Versailles, on the 28th day of June, 1919; and whereas the said treaty of peace was confirmed by the Treaty of Peace Act 1919; and whereas by article 23 of the said treaty the signatories thereto each agreed that they would endeavour to secure and maintain fair and humane conditions of labour for men, women and children, both in their own countries and in all countries to which their commercial and industrial relations extend, and by article 427 of the said treaty it was declared that the well-being, physical, moral and intellectual, of industrial wage-earners is of supreme importance; and whereas a draft convention respecting hours of work in industrial undertakings was agreed upon at a general conference of the internation labour organization of the League of Nations, in accordance with the relevant articles of the said treaty, which said convention has been ratified by Canada; and whereas it is advisable to enact the necessary legislation to enable Canada to discharge the obligations assumed under the provisions of the said treaty and the said convention, and to provide for the limitation of hours of work in industrial undertakings, in accordance with the general provisions of the said convention, and to assist in the maintenance, on equitable terms of interprovineial and international trade.

Will my hon. friend tell me
in a few words what that means?

What I am getting at is that
the whole basis of the present legislation is the treaty obligation into which this country entered, and that in so far as that furnishes the ground of our jurisdiction as a federal parliament to intervene in legislation affecting wages, which in general would come under provincial authority, we must confine our legislation within the general scope of our treaty obligation. We could not go beyond the scope of our treaty obligation without exposing ourselves and exposing this legislation in so far as it goes beyond that scope to the peril of impeachment of our right to pass the legislation at all.

The last speaker said
that the basis of this legislation is our obligation under the treaty of Versailles. What are our obligations under that treaty, according to the preamble of the bill? They are to "endeavour to secure and maintain fair and humane conditions of labour for men, women and children." How are we limited in putting that into effect either by the convention of an international labour body or by any other convention or statute? We cannot be limited except by the extent to which we wish to go. That is the only limit, if this parliament has jurisdiction at all. So that there is no ground whatsoever for the argument the hon. member has just made. AVe are not limited as to the scope of this legislation; we can just as easily extend it. We can bring in or leave out. What we are particularly concerned with is not what has been brought into the bill but what has been left out of it.
The hon. member for Antigonish-Guys-borough made a most extraordinary statement; he said the bill was not necessary because we now have the eight hour day, and if the eight hour day bill was put into effect it would be ruinous. I cannot follow that logic myself. As has already been pointed out by the hon. member for New AVestminster, when legislation of this kind is proposed the argument is always brought forward that if it be put into effect the industries affected will have to close up and quit business. But that has been proved untrue. I ask hon. members how they are going to put back to work some 300,000 heads of families that are now unemployed in this country, and the 20,000 or more who are in camps, if they do not reduce hours of labour? As a matter of fact the people who are working now are supporting those who are not working, and it is only a reasonable suggestion that we should divide the work and let each

Eight Hour Day

one support himself. It is just as well that we should have those who are so ready to protect vested interests come forward now and do their bit, because within a very few weeks or months we shall want to know where they stand anyway.
Owing to the total collapse of the Postmaster General will the hon. member for East Edmonton kindly explain what the hon. member for Vancouver South has been saying to the committee?

I invite the hon. member
to speak for himself.

I understood the hon
member for East Edmonton to say that there is a treaty obligation and therefore we must do this and that. This afternoon at three o'clock the acting Prime Minister read a lengthy answer to a question put some days ago, and in that answer it is shown very clearly and beyond doubt that there is not the slightest obligation upon Canada to stand by that convention. It is merely a suggestion or an earnest wish on the part of the League of Nations; there is no treaty obligation whatever. It is just an occasion for the government to say "we are bound by that," but whether the government says that in a soft voice or in a very loud voice makes no difference; there is no obligation at all upon Canada to stand by that convention. I need not discuss whether this is good or bad, but I look at it from the coercive point of view. Could the league send an army to force Canada to stand by that convention? It could not. The hon. member for East Edmonton knows very well that the league will never send an army to Canada to enforce that convention, so Canada is not bound by it. That appears very clear from the answer given by the acting Prime Minister. Therefore my contention with regard to this bill -I am not discussing whether or not it is good or bad in principle-is that it makes no difference whether or not such conventions have been suggested by the league; this country, as a member of the league, is not bound by them. As my hon. friend from Hochelaga (Mr. St-Pere) said, the best proof of that is that the question will be discussed anew next June. Therefore there is nothing binding Canada in that regard. This is of the utmost importance, because if this country is not bound by that convention-

Have you had your convention in your constituency yet?
[Mr. MacInms.J

No, it is a nomination without a convention. I wonder why this is called a convention. It is more like a formula, a method of procedure, which you may take or leave alone. My hon. friend from Hochelaga says it is an earnest wish, but it is not even a wish; it is just a suggestion. Some members of the government say we are bound by it; such an eminent lawyer as the hon. member for East Edmonton says it is a treaty obligation, but there is no obligation to it. Either it is good or it is bad. If it is bad we should not bother with it, but if it is good it should be enforced. If it is to be enforced that should be done in the proper way. The only means at our disposal to find out if it can be enforced is to ask the opinion of the supreme court, just as we should do in connection with the unemployment insurance bill. Should we speak at any length when we know in advance that this legislation never will be put into operation? Sir, it is just election bait, and I wonder if many electors in this country from the Atlantic to the Pacific will be credulous enough to swallow it. That is all there is to it.
May I suggest that the Minister of Labour and the other members of the government, in the absence of the Prime Minister and the anting Prime Minister, make a decision by themselves in order to show that they are men of good judgment. They are numerous enough to constitute a majority of council, so let them decide that the only way to deal with this matter is to submit the bill to the Supreme Court of Canada now and come to the House of Commons later. If the supreme court says this bill is intra vires I will support it without making any further speeches. If on the other hand the supreme court decide that it is ultra vires of this parliament, then I will respectfully suggest to my hon. friends on the treasury benches that the legislation be dropped. If they take the stand that has been taken by the Prime Minister and the acting Prime Minister we must tell them that they are wasting the time of the house now for Tory propaganda. There are many serious things to consider, such as unemployment relief, and I submit that if they are earnest in their desire for legislation such as this they should have a decision on the matter by the highest tribunal in this country. If they do not do so every member will have the right to say, both inside and outside this house, at any time, that the government are not serious, that they are only trying to fool the people by offering bait of this kind for propaganda purposes.
