Just before this section carries I should like to direct the attention of the minister to one other point in regard to the interpretation clause. If the minister will look at the definition of industrial undertaking he will find that it includes the transport of passengers or goods by road or rail. In reading bill 22, which has to do with the weekly day of rest in industrial undertakings, I find exactly the same words except that in the bill under discussion the words "inland waterway" have been left out. In all other respects the interpretation clause is the same. The inclusion of those words in the bill would mean that the sailors on the great lakes would come under its provisions. If the words were left out in error I submit that the matter should be considered, and in any case I believe these sailors should be included.
Is the minister not going to give us his opinion on the question we raised, in connection with the canneries? It is a most important matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: Perhaps the hon. member was not in the house at the time, but before he spoke on the matter the question was raised by the hon. member ,for Vancouver Centre. I think a cannery falls within the operation of this statute under the interpretation of industrial undertakings. I pointed out, however, that under sections 9 and 10 exceptions could be made and would be made where it was disclosed that an industry was in the position that the hon. member for Gloucester and the hon. member for Vancouver Centre indicated the cannery industry to be in. I thought I made myself clear and I did not think it necessary to repeat my earlier explanation. I may be charged with discourtesy, but I did not intend it in that way.

In my opinion that is not a very strong explanation. It has been said that there are six hundred thousand words in the vocabulary of the English language. Can we not get enough of them to have the bill state exactly what is intended? In connection with another act on Friday we had to trust the whole future of an industry to the question of whether or not it came under the measure. Finally we got it down to this point, that they would be eligible to come under the measure if they could prove themselves to be an anomaly. Let us get away from this indirect system; let us say that this does or does not apply to certain cases. Let us not leave it in the air, and tell an industry that if it can be proved to be an anomaly it may perhaps come under the act. Let us get 0'2582-101i
down in black and white whether or not this measure does apply to a particular industry, especially when it concerns matters of such vital importance as those indicated in the wire I read a few moments ago. I have not left the house since three o'clock, so it was not through any negligence on my part that I did not hear the explanation the minister said he gave to the hon. member for Vancouver Centre. The minister now states that a remedy would be found under sections 9 and 10 of the bill. He has stated that canneries would come under section 2, and would be eligible for the operation of eight hour regulations, but he states further that there is provision in sections 9 and 10 for taking the canneries out from under such legislation. If it is abundantly evident, as I think it must be, that canneries cannot be operated under eight hour legislation, why trust to the indirect method of wriggling them out under some regulation yet to be born, under virtue of sections 9 and 10? Why not state dearly under section 2 that the fishing industry shall not be affected by the eight hour legislation?
We turn to section 9 and we are told that somehow they will be able to wriggle out under the provisions to be made thereunder. Section 9 states:
The governor in council may, in exceptional cases-
There is nothing exceptional about the fishing industry. The condition whereby there is an inability to accept eight-hour shifts is one which exists all the time. However this section states:
The governor in council may, in exceptional cases where it is recognized that the daily limit of hours of work cannot be applied and agreements between workers' and employers' organizations to increase the daily limit have been made, give effect to such agreements and permit in such cases the said daily limit of hours to be exceeded: Provided, however that the average number of hours per week over the number of weeks covered by any such agreement shall not exceed forty-eight.
The ordinary fish or pilchard plant is not of the type which could readily be brought under the provisions of section 9. There are no organized bodies of cannery employees; they are entirely transient. Certainly they could not make agreements with the employers to which the government could give sanction. The wording of the section could not apply to these workers.
Now we come to section 10, and we find that
it states:
The governor in council may also make regulations permitting

(a) permanent exceptions to the limits of hours of work fixed by this act in case of preparatory or complementary work which must
Eight Hour Day

necessarily be carried on outside the limits laid down for the general working of an establishment, ...
We find the expression "outside the limits," and, mark you, the conditions of making permanent exceptions to the limits of hours of work must be cases of "preparatory or complementary work" which must be carried on outside the limits laid down for the general working of an establishment. In other words, there must be something extraordinary, or something which would occur only very intermittently, such as cleaning out boilers of a plant. Operations of this type would have to be done perhaps only once a month, or once a fortnight. But these operations must be carried on "outside the limits laid down." The ordinary limits laid down in the instance I have in mind, or the ordinary work involved, is that of men going out and bringing in perhaps eight tons of fish to-day and eight hundred tons to-morrow. That catch has to be handled before it goes bad. Those are the ordinary conditions which obtain, and I suggest one could not construe the words "preparatory or complementary work" as applying to the ordinary conditions of canning fish. Therefore I believe that argument knocks out the first part of paragraph (a). Then we find the further expression:
Or for certain clases of workers whose work is essentially intermittent.
That might apply to certain people whose work may be that of putting labels on tins only at certain intervals, but I say a person could not go through a cannery and say, "This class shall work under the eight hour day regulations, and these other chaps shall not." One cannot say, "This class must come under the operation of section 2 of the act, and this chap, over here, can get an exemption because his work is intermittent." A cannery must be operated as a complete unit. The general conditions connected with running a fish plant are such that it cannot be operated under eight hour day regulations, and I defy any hon. member in this chamber to say that he would attempt to do so. If I am correct, why have such provisions in the act? Why pile up trouble? Why pile Pelion on Ossa? Why say, "We are going to place you under the operations of the act, but if you can climb out from under by the strained and drastic interpretation of sections 9 and 10 perhaps you will get the relief to which you are undoubtedly entitled?" Either they are, or they are not, entitled to relief. If it is so that certain classes cannot work under the eight hour day regulations, why not say so frankly?

I fully agree with the observations which have been made by hon. members sitting to my left in which they have described the advantages derived from working only eight hours. I know of an instance where a big plant was told that it would be placed under the provisions of legislation passed by a provincial government, that eight hour day legislation was going to be put into effect, and the result was that in that one plant alone nineteen more men were given work. What was the attitude of the employers? They said, "We do not mind, because we get more work in shorter hours." They found they could get better work and that there would be less accidents, as the hon. member for Pictou said, when the men were working only eight hours. How can we help the operation of the act if we compel people to come under its provisions who, nature and common sense tell us, cannot possibly operate under them? Why not leave this section over so that the minister may consider it? Let him get the advice of his friends from British Columbia. A great canning and reducing industry has been developed in that province and surely it is entitled to be heard. Their present Relief is that the wording of section 2 does not bring them within the operation of the measure. If it does,-well, at least tell them so and give them twenty-four hours to make their representations.

May I point out that the legislation in British Columbia provides, in chapter 30, section 11, paragraph 2 (a):
(a) The permanent exceptions that may be allowed in preparatory or complementary work which must necessarily be carried on outside the limits laid down for the general working of an industrial undertaking, or for certain classes of workers whose work is essentially seasonal or intermittent.
And so on. I would indicate to the minister that in this legislation the word "seasonal" appears.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: It will be recalled that earlier in the afternoon I informed the committee that I had had sections 9 and 10 under consideration, with a view to having proposed an amendment enabling the governor in council to make regulations which would take care of the various industrial activities to which reference has been made.

But this is too much work for the government, and we want to make those regulations ourselves. We want them to be made in the House of Commons so that we may know what they are.

Eight Hour Day

Mr. Chairman, some time ago I accepted the explanation given by the Minister of Trade and Commerce to the effect that fishermen could claim exemption under sections 9 and 10. Looking through the sections however I find tlxat no applications for exemptions can foe made except in certain ways, namely by organizations of employers or by organizations of employees. If that is the only way in which subsection 2 of section 10 can be dealt with, then1 I say it cannot apply because in many sections of the country there are no such things as organizations of employees and organizations of employers. Something else must be inserted in the clause to give the government the right to act upon the application of parties in the business who do not belong to organizations. I trust the ministry will take that point into consideration, because it is an important one.
If the act is made applicable to the fishing industry let me say to the minister and to hon. members of the committee that despite the views held by the hon. member for East Hamilton, and despite the fact that I may be upbraided by him for my observations, the fishing industry will be ruined. The government of Canada passes certain regulations governing the fishing industry. For instance, they fix the season for lobster canning, for salmon canning, and so on. Those industries are seasonal, and I am wondering if during the canning seasons the government is going to restrict the working hours, because if they are they are going to put the industry out of business. That observation applies not only to canning but to other branches of the fishing industry. For instance, the operations connected with dried salt cod are seasonal. The vessels which go to the cod banks may stay away all week, and upon returning home on Saturday the fishermen have to work at nights, and sometimes on Sundays, to unload their vessels. They have to do that, irrespective of hours, to save their catch and place it where it can be prepared for the market. If this legislation becomes effective they could not do so; they would be confined to certain hours of labour and the progress ,of the industry would be seriously hampered and perhaps destroyed. I would ask the minister if at all possible to give us something definite so far as the fishing industry is concerned. I am entirely in agreement with the principle of the measure. I am for an eight hour day law, but not for an act which will give eight hours a day to a certain class of industry and destroy another industry perhaps more important than the one protected.

Coming from British Columbia, I must associate myself to a certain degree with the hon. member for Comox-Alberni in pointing out that it would be disastrous to the canning industry of British Columbia were an eight hour day to be enforced. There is no one in the house more in favour of an eight hour day than I am. I believe the day is coming when we shall have a five hour day; if we are to put the unemployed to work in Canada'-and the same is true of the United States-we must reduce the hours of labour. I can quite understand however that at the present time we must move slowly, because we do not wish to hamper those who are engaged in manufacturing for export to other countries. It would be suicidal if we were to make any very drastic reduction in the hours of labour below eight hours. In British Columbia eight hours have been considered a day's work, but the British Columbia government wisely exempted the canning industry, the fisheries and ship yards from the eight hour law. AVith the ship yards there are many arguments in favour of exemption, but I see under section 10, where work is considered intermittent, they may be allowed to work longer hours. As regards the canning industry, the canning of salmon, I think we should be able to tell the cannery men definitely that they will not come under the eight hour law. They get a lot of fish one day and work from ten to fifteen hours and then they loaf two or three days before getting another consignment. They are a long way from the labour market, operating on the northern coast of British Columbia, and it would necessitate two crews, which they could not afford. I am satisfied from the minister's promise that he will frame an amendment which will take care of this phase of the question. I leave it at that.

The minister says that he
will put in regulations, or rather he will put in power under which it may be possible to make regulations with respect to the exemption of the fishing industry. But as the hon. member for Nanaimo has pointed out, that is not what we require. What those engaged in the fishing industry are asking for is a definite announcement. A great many people in British Columbia, like the salmon people, have to be financed by the banks, and I doubt whether the bank would finance this industry if they had to trust to its exemption from this legislation under some regulation still to be conceived in the mind of someone not yet appointed. What these people want is an assurance which they can give to the banks, because the bank will not advance money to the industry on any other terms. It is
Eight Hour Day

necessary to make certain preparations, to charter boats, hire fishermen and so on, because you do not start fishing on a sudden impulse, as you play golf some afternoon; it takes months of preparation and the expenditure of thousands of dollars for nets, tins and so on. It is not an idle suggestion that the industry would be much happier in going to the bank if they could assure the bank that there was an exemption definitely provided for in the bill rather than the promise that some regulation not yet framed might be drafted.

Subsection (d) reads:
Transport of passengers or goods by road or rail, including the handling of goods at docks, quays, wharves or warehouses, but excluding transport by hand.
Let me submit the railway employees' case. They are often on duty when on a return trip. Sometimes they are twelve, fourteen and twenty hours at a time and it counts for the number of hours they are supposed to be working during the month. The minister knows how the time of railway men is calculated. How will he manage to apply this legislation to railway employees when they are on duty on a return trip? May I ask him to answer that question?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: The position of railway men raises of course a difficult question. I have given it a good deal of consideration and I believe that an amendment which I shall have to suggest in connection with the regulations under section 10 will take care of the difficulty, which is an obvious one.

I thank the hon. gentleman, but up to now we have heard several complaints from different corners of the house in regard to this legislation, and if there are so many exemptions that it does not apply to anyone, what is the use of passing it? May I tell the government once more that it is most dangerous to bring in new legislation of this kind when it is half-baked. I do not blame the Minister of Labour, and he knows that. But very often such legislation is brought down in such a condition that it is impossible to know what is behind it, and there are clauses which contradict one another. And even this legislation contradicts regulations with regard to fishing. It renders the understanding of the law more difficult than ever. Everyone is supposed to be familiar with the law, because ignorance of the law is no legal excuse. It is very hard to understand all these provisions. I suggest to the minister that he take time to study this legislation by himself. He is a lawyer of
tMr. Neill.]
considerable experience and he knows much more than the third rate clerks who drafted the legislation. I insist on that. Here is a man who was responsible for the worst piece of legislation, the War Time Elections Act of 1917-something awful-and he was brought into service again for the gerrymander legislation. He is putting his nose and his fingers into this legislation again, spoiling the statute book of this coimtry, wherever we find his fingerprints. I do not want the government to look after that man, who has very badly drafted legislation to his credit, if I may say so, and to call him again to draft this legislation on so-called social order. I would ask the government to let the legislation mature for a time so that it may improve like wine. Wine improves while it matures, and I am very optimistic when I make that suggestion. As it is, it is an awful mess and that is why I oppose it strongly. I am in favour of the principle of it, but I am strongly against the letter, which is so bad. May I suggest to the minister that he kindly take time to study this legislation himself, to see how contradictory it is, and after he discovers this, to clear his conscience by submitting it to the Supreme Court of Canada, who will undoubtedly decide that it is ultra vires of this parliament.

The question has been asked by an hon. member as to why, since the wording of the convention itself has been followed almost entirely throughout the subsections of section 2, the words "sea and inland waterways" were left out, thereby excluding from the operation of this legislation the workers engaged in these two particular industries. It is particularly significant that they should be excluded, when we remember that there are few nations that carry on so large a business on and derive so large a living from inland waterways as Canada. Can the minister explain why these words are left out?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: I cannot.

Here we have a minister,
one of the ablest lawyers in this country, who makes that answer. We have not his experience and we want some enlightenment on this bill, which is so badly drafted that even a lawyer of the great experience of the minister is unable to give a satisfactory explanation to the back benchers in this house. We want a satisfactory explanation about it. We have to decide what will be done in accordance with the legislation. If the hon. gentleman who is piloting the bill through the committee does not know the intent of it, how can we vote for it? The

Eight Hour Day
situation is most peculiar; no ope understands anything about the matter. This reminds me of the time when I was in college and our professor said to us: "When you do not understand something I am teaching you of philosophy and if I feel that I do not understand it myself, it is metaphysics." Well, this legislation must be metaphysics to the Minister of Labour. No one in the committee understands anything about the provision; how then can we vote for it? There are several hon. members opposite who all look well informed; they may be well informed about everything but this. They do not understand this provision; they do not know where it leads. Even the minister who is supposed to throw light on the matter says: "Well, stay in the darkness." Let them call O'Connor at once; let them page him and ask him what is behind this provision. I want information; I am not going to vote for this provision unless I understand its meaning and if we do not know, what will the judges decide when they have to interpret the intent of the law maker when the law maker himself has no intent at all except "win the election"- and we give credit to the government for that noble thought. We are the highest court in this country; we have to pass legislation which will apply to hundreds of thousands of people and is of great moment. We ask for light, but there is none; the sun is hiding himself behind the mountain; it is after dusk and the sun has disappeared.
The Minister of Labour has a great sense of humour, and he understands how ridiculous it is for us to have to argue on legislation which cannot be explained by anyone. Can you bell me, Mr. Chairman, what is behind this provision? You do not know any more than I do. Then let us call for Mr. O'Connor at once. Otherwise, what will the judges say? I see the dignified judges sitting on the bench and saying; " What about this? We do not understand." What will happen? If this legislation stands and is voted upon in this way, the House of Commons will be laughed at, not only by the judges but by every citizen who will see the performance before the court when the latter will have to interpret this provision. The situation is most absurd; it is so absurd that it is incredible. It would take Courte-line to describe such a situation. It is incredible that in this house no one knows what a provision of a bill, submitted to the house means. In that case let us drop it; let us turn the page and look for something . else. Until a satisfactory explanation is given, I do not see how we can proceed any further with this abominable legislation.
How will it settle the social evils from which this country at present suffers? No one knows. It is impossible to know. If the Minister of Labour were not such an able lawyer-and I am glad to pay him that tribute-I would say: Well, it has been put into his hands and he does not know. But he is one of the foremost lawyers of this country and he does not know. How then can an ordinary mortal explain the whole matter? All the members of the committee are laughing at the situation. It is ridiculous and I strongly protest against it. I regret the government has hired the services of that man who has put into their hands such awful legislation. I wonder how it will work for election propaganda afterwards. Just a little pin on the balloon and, pouf! nothing is left; it falls to the ground. The minister himself will see that he cannot insist upon the passing of this legislation. I have respect for his experience at the bar, but I see hon. members opposite looking very sad now because the minister cannot explain the legislation. It cannot be explained and they all look so sad. I do not want them to cry, but I do not want them to insist any more upon our passing such ridiculous and incredible legislation.

To revert
to paragraph (d) of clause 2: the minister was kind enough a moment ago to tell me that he did not know, nor could he explain, why the words of the convention itself "sea or inland waterways" were let out of that clause. Would he accept the inclusion of the words now since they are part of the original convention?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: The exclusion of the words "sea or inland waterways" which appear in the convention may have been brought about for a good reason. So far as I am concerned I overlooked the fact that they were dropped in the clause of the bill, and that fact was not drawn pointedly to my attention. Rather than have them included now without having an opportunity to inform myself whether there is some sound reason for having them deleted from the bill when they appear in the convention, I would prefer to have the clause stand.

I think
that would be just as well, and whilst the clause stands, I hope the minister will take into consideration again the possibility of including restaurant and hotel workers and employees in chain stores under the inclusive clauses (a), Ob) or (c). Personally, I believe they can all be brought in under (bl under

the provisions of the convention. I think the convention itself provides a very easy method by which the government could include the industries to which I have referred. He will find that the very last sentence in article I of the convention reads:
The competent authority in each country shall define the line of division which separates industry from commerce and agriculture.
Therefore this government, having assumed it is the competent authority to . legislate in keeping with the convention, should have no difficulty under its provisions in including such industries as have been mentioned this afternoon. I hope they will be taken into consideration.

It will stand before the
committee until it falls before the court.

Section 2 agreed to.
On section 3-Eight hours in the day, forty-eight in the week.

Because one points out defects in the bill he is not necessarily opposed to it. I am in favour of it, and for two reasons in particular. I think that in the modem intensively operated factory men can exhaust themselves in eight hours of work. Another reason is that it is generally accepted by working people that this bill if adopted will mean that more people will have work. But I am not sure that the bill has been safeguarded properly. I am afraid its purpose may be defeated by the workmen themselves. It contains no provision limiting the hours a man may work. We had instances during war time when: factories were working twenty-four hours a day in three eight hour shifts, of men working eight hours in one factory and hurrying to another and working there eight hours more. And they did it for some length of time. At this time such outstanding instances as that may not occur, but consider for example carpenters or painters. A carpenter may work eight hours and then take on contract work or odd jobs after the day's work is done. The same thing may be done by painters. I think the bill should have a clause in it providing that men cannot work beyond eight hours 'for hire, gain or pay. Of course it would be impossible and undesirable not to permit men to work on their own property, but it seems to me that

if the full benefit of the bill is to be obtained that feature will have to be dealt with. I should like an expression of opinion from the minister concerning that.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
The hon. member raises a very important question. At the moment I would not care to express an opinion on it. If the hon. member would like the section to stand I will give it thought to see what can be done.
Section 3 stands.
Section 2 also stood.
No, it was carried.
The minister stated before recess that section 2 would stand.
It was carried after eight o'clock.
It was to stand for consideration and explanation. The Minister of Railways was here and heard the Minister of Labour state in answer to questions from this side that it should stand.
No, I was not here then.

Well, it was to stand in order that we might have some explanation, notably in regard to the exclusion of certain industries, and also in connection with the leaving out of the words "inland waterways."

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
During the dinner hour I looked into the question of the deletion of the words "by sea and inland waterways" from the bill. They appeared in the original convention. I have before me and am reading from the article, where it is stated that:
The provisions relative to transport by sea and on inland waterways shall be determined by a special conference dealing with employment at sea and on inland waterways.
The competent authority in each country shall define the line of division which separates industry from commerce and agriculture.
With respect to transport by sea and inland waterways, two conferences were held, one in 1920 and one in 1929. At these conferences all the member states were represented and it was found utterly impossible to come to an agreement as to limiting hours of labour in transport by sea or inland waterways. This undoubtedly is the reason why it was omitted from the bill. The convention itself was adopted subject to transport by sea and inland waterways being left open to see if the

Eight Hour Day
member states could come to a unanimous decision, which as yet they have not been able to do.

Surely the [DOT] minister does not suggest that we in Canada must delay action in the application of the eight hour day to any particular industry until we get unanimous consent from other nations. That would be a ridiculous position to take. We have to take our own steps and be responsible for them. These words were in the convention and were agreed to and accepted by Canada, and this legislation is supposed to be based on a convention which was solemnly signed and accepted.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: Subject to what I have just said.
May I ask if the minister has given further consideration to the question of the inclusion of restaurant and hotel workers?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: Yes I have, and my view is that by going to the length suggested, and enlarging the convention upon which this bill is based, we would probably strengthen materially the position of those who might seek to have the bill declared ultra vires of this parliament. When we are embarking on legislation of this kind I think we should not adopt a course calculated to destroy the measure itself.

Section agreed to.
Sections 4 to 8 inclusive agreed to.
On section 9-Exceptional cases.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
With respect to sections 9 and 10, I listened to what was said by hon. members with regard to certain industries, and their criticism of section 10 particularly. I would like these two sections to stand until I give them further consideration, to ensure that there shall be authority to except industries which by their nature could not operate- as both employers and employees want them to operate, because it is so easy at times to impede an industry-particularly industries such as those to which reference was made before the dinner hour.
Sections 9 and 10 stand.
Sections 11 to 13 inclusive agreed to.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
It is my view that there should be a further section added to the bill. I have not the amendment written out, but it will be a short one, having to do with the date on which the bill shall become operative.
As the bill now reads it will become operative upon receiving the royal assent. In order that industries affected by the measure shall be able to make adjustments, which undoubtedy they will have to make, I think it would be unwise not to give them some period of time before the penal section might apply. I had not given a great deal of thought to the question how long the period should be. Someone suggested six months; I think that is too long. Probably three months would be ample. If any hon. member has any view to express with respect to that point I should like to hear it.
Six months would get us past an election.
Three months.

I should like to ask the minister if it might not be worth his while, now that he is not going to have the penal sections of the act come into force for several months, to consider whether in the interval he might not get an opinion from the supreme court as to whether or not the act itself is intra vires. Advantage might be taken of that interval of time to remove all possibility of doubt as to the competence of this parliament to enact the legislation.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: I do not think I would care to sponsor the submission of that question even to the Supreme Court of Canada. I entertain the view that in projecting legislation this parliament should not first seek the authority of any judicial tribunal as to whether such legislation is intra vires or ultra vires of the dominion parliament. I may be wrong in that, but I am afraid that if this policy were pursued we would not advance legislation very rapidly through parliament Perhaps we are on sounder ground if we take the position that if anyone seeks to impeach this measure, then upon the issue being raised we can find out the extent to which we acted within our competence in the adoption of the underlying principle and the bill itself.

Is the Minister of Labour aware of the fact that certain legislative assemblies are introducing eight hour bills? Has that been drawn to his attention? The other day I noticed that in the speech from the throne at the opening of the legislature of Nova Scotia the lieutenant governor stated that they intended to introduce an eight hour measure. Is it necessary for both the legislatures and this parliament to introduce eight hour legislation, or which has power to do so? Has the minister considered that point?
Eight Hour Day

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: I am aware that a majority of the provinces have legislation limiting the hours of work, and I think there is no insuperable barrier in the way of the provinces and the dominion, if they work in cooperation, making these measures work side by side, or where one fails the other may be applied without confusion. I know of the legislation in the various provinces.
I was wondering, if parliament passes this act, if it would be necessary for the provinces to pass similar legislation.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: It might not be.

Would the minister tell the committee exactly the process by which he expects this act to be enforced? Will there be an inspection by officers appointed by this government, officers of the Department of Labour, or will there be a special staff set up under the regulations?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: My view is that the services of some one or more of the present departments of government might well be utilized in the administration of this act. I am very hopeful that we will find a great majority of employers and employees joining to render this act a useful piece of legislation. Of course in all matters of this kind officers have to see to it that the comparatively small number of employers who might do so-I think I am justified in saying so-are not permitted to do violence to this act and that, if they do so, they suffer the consequences contemplated by the act. That is a matter that will have to be given immediate attention in order that the act may be administered with the least possible expense, having regard to efficient administration.

But what I am really trying to get at is this. Suppose an infraction of the act is reported. To whom in the first place should it be reported and, after it is reported, who will take the necessary steps to prosecute and punish the employer?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
Section 13 of the act, the penal section, reads:
Every employer who violates, or fails or omits to comply with any provision of this act or of any regulation made thereunder, shall for each offence be liable on summary conviction-
That of course means that he will be proceeded against under the summary conviction sections of the criminal code. The law may be set in motion by anyone.
Anyone?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: By anyone, I should think. Of course it is the duty of every citizen, although everyone does not discharge that duty to the full, if he knows there has been a breach of a law, to set the law in motion. That is the theory, though sometimes the theory does not work out. In this case a great many people will be interested; the employee, his labour organization, the inspectors of the department, whoever they may be, or some officer of one of the departments that may be available to check up, supervise and see to the enforcement of the act-all these will be interested to see that the act is carried out. At the moment it would be impossible for me to say just who would set the law in motion, but any one of those I have enumerated could do so. Of course the government must see that there are those charged with the responsibility of seeing that the law is enforced.

I am sorry but the minister leaves the whole position even worse than it is under provincial legislation to-day. As the minister knows, there have been violations of all these laws in connection with factory hours, minimum wages and hours of labour in almost every province in which they have been brought into being. The evidence given before the price spreads committee shows the flagrant violations in both Ontario and Quebec in regard to minimum wage legislation, for example, and no one seems to have had the responsibility of taking action against the offending employers. There is no use in saying that it is left to the employee, because in nine oases out of ten the employee is afraid of losing his or her job and will not individually, sometimes not even collectively, take the necessary action. Therefore I strongly suggest to the minister that this act should provide for an official inspector, or you can call him a public prosecutor if you like, to whom infractions of the act should be reported, who should investigate and, upon finding the reports to be correct, should take action on behalf of the employee. I also think the expenses in connection with administration should be borne by the government.
Will this act be administered directly by the Department of Labour?

speechtext:

In view of the fact that there is legislation before the house having to do with the weekly day of rest, may I ask the Secretary of State if there is any truth in the statement made in one of the newspapers of Ottawa that the workers in the printing bureau are working on Sundays in the preparation of voters lists? If that condition exists I am sure the minister could not have known about it, because as a member of the church to which I give my allegiance I am sure he would not for one moment permit a condition under which men in the printing bureau worked seven days a week, or more than eight hours a day.

The hon. gentleman, the

Item agreed to.
International office for the protection of industrial property, international copyright union office and union for the protection of literary and artistic works, $2,600.

May we
have an explanation of the reason for the expenditure? What is done through this vote?

Canada is one of the members of the international union for the protection of industrial property. That is a body for the protection of copyrights, trade marks, patents and designs, and under the convention
Supply-Secretary oj State

to which we are a party we pay a certain proportion of the expense of the international office maintained at Berne in Switzerland. If the hon. member wishes full details I could give them, but may I state briefly that this is an annual vote. The slight decrease of $250 is due to the appreciation of the dollar as compared with the value of the Swiss franc.

I was
familiar with the facts the Secretary of State has given, but I should like to know of what value the international office is to Canada. What do we get for the expenditure?

The convention has been
subscribed to and ratified by about forty nations, if my recollection is correct, and from time to time the representatives of the several nations meet at Washington, Rome, or London, England, to discuss changes in the convention for the protection of industrial property. One matter, which will be under a discussion, when the Patent bill is before the house in a few days, is that as Canada is a party to the convention, inventors in Canada have the right to have Canadian patents of invention registered in each of these foreign countries, in which event they obtain the same protection and privileges as were granted upon application for and the grant of such patents in Canada. Similar provisions are in the convention in respect of trade marks. I think it was two years ago that I introduced and there was enacted the Unfair Competition Act dealing with trade marks, which is based on the same convention; and trade marks which are granted in Canada to those doing business and using those trade marks in Canada are by the terms of the convention protected in each of these other countries.
Are there any major countries that do not protect patents?

I had in my hand during

Why should there be two separate items, one for National Defence and one under the Secretary of State, in connection with the adjustment of war claims?

At the close of the war the Department of the Secretary of State was vested with jurisdiction in all matters relating to reparations and the sequestration of enemy property, which included certain war claims. Those claims with regard to reparations have been, I think, completely disposed of and Germany, as the house knows, has ceased making the payments which were to be made under the treaty of Versailles. I am putting in this sum simply to cover any possible contingencies that may arise in regard to past inquiries and matters of that kind.
I understand that the sum will not necessarily be expended and that there are now no outstanding claims under this vote.

I made a return to the house, to-day I think, showing that there were two or three contingent claims aggregating less than $5,000, which are outstanding and unpaid. I understand that these are claims of sailors who were on ships that were destroyed by German torpedoes or sunk by mines. These sailors made claims-three of four of them- and since the awards have been made we have

Item agreed to.
Oyster culture, $10,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence

So far seventy-nine leases comprising nearly 344 acres

That does not seem to

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
The information I have
at my disposal at the moment is that only two permits are granted to each lessee. The matter can very easily be verified; we can look it up. I have not the information in more detail now.

I may have been wrongly informed, but I understand that not only can the holder of the lease obtain two permits, but all those working for him or members of his family can also obtain permits, so that all one has to do is to have an application for a lease and then one can get permits to pick all the oysters he likes off the public ground. I think this is something that should be looked into very carefully, because I know it is causing a great deal of dissatisfaction. The public fishermen feel that public oyster areas should be developed by the department for public fishing, but the department has undertaken to lease those public areas to private individuals. Since the Richmond bay area was known for its famous oysters the public were always allowed to fish off the public beds there. Now the department has started on this policy of leasing, and the greatest difficulty we find is that areas which are producing oysters at the present time are being leased, or, if not, the oyster picked off for private holders. I know the department will deny this, but the fishermen have asked for a royal commission; they have even petitioned the governor general in council to have a commission or someone appointed to go down there and make a thorough investigation of the whole situation. This has been refused by the department. The fishermen are deprived of fishing privileges which they formerly enjoyed. I have on my desk a petition which has been presented in which they say that if the department is going to spend money to bring back the areas for private individuals it is only fair to spend some money

Supply-Fisheries
to bring back some areas for public fishing. The fishermen would not object much if the department would go out into the deeper bays and rivers where oysters are not coming back satisfactorily and there build up fishing areas for those who obtain private leases, but they do object to leasing the inshore waters in the small rivers and bays and he-ads of creeks where the oysters are coming bade naturally and where they could fish with very little trouble. If the department wants to experiment there are thousands of acres out in the big bays and rivers where they can spend all the money they like in bringing back the beds for the private lessee. But the claim is made, and I think fairly, that the fishermen have an inherent right, handed down from .past generations, to fish on the public areas. I know the minister will say: Well, the industry was wiped out and we had to come and reestablish it. The industry was wiped out; now it is coming back naturally at the heads of the rivers and bays, and what we object to is the leasing of those areas where the industry shows signs of natural recovery. We all know that at tire present time fishermen are hard pressed, not only in our province but in other provinces where fishing is carried on. In this industry men were formerly able to go out and make a fair day's pay with very little expense. About $10 or $15 will fit out a fisherman for gathering oysters, whereas if he is going into the lobster industry, for instance, he has to spend hundreds of' dollars for equipment. The fishermen feel that this privilege has been taken away from them. They have petitioned, the department; they have done everything they could to get some attention, to have someone go there and make an independent survey and see if their claims are well founded.
I had to bring up this matter last year. I do not want to be blocking the work of the department, but I think in all fairness to the fishermen of that community the department should have someone go and make a thorough examination on the spot. I know the department will say that they are not leasing areas that are already productive, but the fishermen have the opposite view. They say that no one applying for a private lease will take a piece of ground unless he is pretty sure that there are some oysters on that ground. If he finds there are, then he is willing to take a lease. They also complain that the public areas that would naturally come back are being robbed by private lessees who are given permits to pick oysters off the public grounds to put on their private grounds. So in effect the fishermen are not allowed to fish
at all unless they have a lease. This is a revolutionary step on the part of the department and is so entirely at variance with the conditions that formerly obtained that the fishermen are up in arms about it. I would like to put on record a great many statements that have been forwarded to me, and also this petition, but I have submitted a similar one to the minister, and all without avail. I am a voice crying in the wilderness; I get no support from the department or from other hon. members from our province or from the acting Minister of Fisheries, and fail to make any impression on the department on behalf of the large number of fishermen whom I represent in this house. But I submit that their demand is fair and just and that the new minister who is now in this responsible position should give the matter very careful consideration and see that justice is done to these fishermen who are not here to speak for themselves and who have been unable through petition or otherwise to make any impression on the department or the minister.

You perhaps will remember, Mr. Chairman, that last session the same annual complaint was made by my hon. friend from Prince. The hon. member has a monopoly on this subject; there does not seem to be anyone else here sufficiently interested in oyster culture to make a study of the matter so as to be able to answer him. I rise on this occasion with more than usual diffidence because I have not forgotten the severe castigation I received at the hands of the hon. member for Prince last session when this same item was before the committee. On that occasion I was told that I was an inlander, that I did not know anything about fish, and above all about oysters, and I was advised to confine my activities to the growing of potatoes. I can assure the committee that my hon. friend's advice was not lost on your humble servant, and I do not intend to-night to advance any of my own ideas along this line for fear of receiving again the same admonition from my hon. friend. I do not wish to detam the committee more than a few minutes. I only want to say that in my humble opinion as an onlooker from the outside, seeing what the Department of Fisheries has done during the past few years for the oyster industry in Prince Edward Island, I cannot help but raise my voice in commendation of the acting Minister of Fisheries and especially of his able deputy minister for the efficient efforts
Supply-Fisheries

they have put forth on behalf of the oyster industry of Prince Edward Island. In order that I may be quite clear on this matter I have on this occasion armed myself with a report of a speech that was delivered by a man who-even the hon. member for Prince will not deny it-is one of the leading fishery experts in Prince Edward Island. We have in Charlottetown a very active board of trade. No item affecting the public good escapes their attention-agriculture, business, fisheries, tourist traffic, everything of that kind comes under their purview. They are always very active in finding out what is being done along these lines. In order to inform themselves thoroughly on this subject, to get the best information they could, they invited W. F. Tidmarsh to speak to them, which he did on January 10 last. By the way, let me state a fact well known to the hon. member for Prince. In addition to being an expert in connection with fisheries and everything pertaining to the fishing industry in Prince Edward Island, having been engaged in that industry all his life, Mr. W. F. Tidmarsh is also one of the leading Liberals in our province, a fact which must carry great weight with my hon. friend. At the present time his son is president of the Liberal Association of Queens county, and I believe the father is just as active as ever on that side of politics. I would not be too sure of that, however; he may have had a change of heart since January 10, when the Prime Minister came out with his reform program. Mr. Tidmarsh, along with many other Liberals of Prince Edward Island, may have had a change of heart since then, so it would not surprise me to find him lined up behind the Prime Minister, myself and my colleague when the next election comes along. But without wearying the committee further I should like to quote briefly what Mr. Tidmarsh said to the Charlottetown board of trade on January 10 last:
Commends Department Effort
The effort of the fishery department to restore the oyster fishery is well worthy of favourable commendation.
Those are the words of the leading Liberal of Prince Edward Island.
It has worked in a thoroughly scientific manner. It has erected and operated' at Bideford river a small biological laboratory, equipped with necessary equipment, and in it has placed men of scientific and practical knowledge

And now the hon. gentleman wants somebody to go down there from Ottawa, when right in his own bailiwick they have this biological

laboratory containing the necessary equipment, with men of scientific and practical knowledge in charge. Is that not enough for him?
-who are applying themselves solely to experimentation in oyster culture, to demonstrate that oysters may be cultivated on a commercially economic basis.
Several sections of barren bottoms-
That is barren enough for anything.

were selected in Richmond and Malpeque bays, where the famous Malpeque oyster once thrived. Each bed contains about four and a half acres. These beds were seeded with small oysters. The results have been highly satisfactory.
At the opening of the fishing season this fall it was estimated that approximately each acre had produced eight hundred bushels of marketable oysters. I am informed that the product of these beds is sold on the open market, and the proceeds credited to the beds, so that the commercial value may be ascertained.
Just notice this next paragraph:
Leasing System Beneficial
Areas of five and a half acres of barren bottom may be leased from the fishery department for a period of twenty years, at $1 per acre, per annum, for the first period, and for the second period at a rental to be agreed upon. The lessee agrees to seed the areas within a reasonable time.
This method should meet with general approval.
I believe the word "general" would include even the hon. member for Prince.
It assures a wide distribution of oyster farming throughout the province, keeps the industry in the hands of our fishermen-
I hope the hon. member for Prince will note that.
-encourages competition, stimulates enterprise, and ensures a wide distribution of the monetary returns when the areas become productive.
This industry lends itself to cooperation of the primary producer. Fishermen should be encouraged to form cooperative companies. The combined efforts of a small company of young, energetic fishermen, should in a few years create an industry, under their own control, that would give them remunerative employment for the rest of their lives.
Over-production need not be feared. Epicures through the ages' have sought this succulent bivalve and will continue to do so in the future....
I see no reason to doubt that the oyster fishery will, in process of time, become the most important fishing industry in this province.
I have not touched on the technique of oyster culture. Prospective cultivators can get that information by applying to the biological station at Bideford-
Just imagine; they can get all the information with reference to oyster culture at this biological station at Bideford, in the riding of my hon. friend who is objecting to the whole development.

Supply-Fisheries
-or by consulting a book entitled Oyster Farming on the Atlantic Coast of Canada, published by the Department of Fisheries.
I have no further remarks to make. Hon. gentlemen will notice that for fear of a second castigation at the hands of my hon. friend 1 have sheltered myself behind the words of a Prince Edward Island gentleman who has forgotten more about oysters and the fishing industry than the hon. member for Prince and myself together know.

In reply to my hon. friend I may say that I am perfectly willing to give him all the latitude he requires, because the more latitude he takes the deeper he gets in. My hon. friend has said that Mr. Tidmarsh satisfactorily explained this matter to the board of trade. I have known Mr. Tidmarsh for a great many years. I have known him as a lobster packer of outstanding ability; I have known him to be interested in the processing and marketing of other kinds of fish, but this is the first intimation I have had that Mr. Tidmarsh is an authority on oysters or oyster culture, and I thank my hon. friend from Queens for that illuminating fact. My hon. friend suggested that Mr. Tidmarsh might have changed his politics following the radio addresses of the Prime Minister. I am afraid my hon. friend will have to wait for some time for that. I think oysters will be growing under the potato vines in his fields before that happens.
The difficulty in this whole situation is that people like my good friend, who would like to know all about the industry but has never taken the trouble to make himself thoroughly acquainted with it, are always butting in and giving advice to the department. As I have said before, some people step in where angels fear to tread. The situation, nevertheless, is as I have stated. I do not wish to discuss this matter from a political point of view, but I want my hon. friend from Queens to understand that it was at the request of myself and others that the biological station was started at Bideford under the Liberal administration. The Liberal policy, however, was to bring back the oyster industry for the public fishermen of that community; we never intended to give a private monopoly to any other class of men, and we stand by that policy to-day. I believe that I am voicing the opinion of hon. members of this house and of the majority of the fishermen of our province when I say that the rights of our fishermen are being taken away under this leasing policy.
With regard to the biological station, the men located there are doing work that has been assigned to them, that is, studying the habits and the propagation of oysters, and
oyster culture. They have made certain progress along that line, but I am not here to-night to discuss whether or not the biological station has been of service to the fishermen or the industry; I am here to discuss the right of the fishermen to fish in the public waters around their own shores. If the department wants to lease ground there are thousands of acres, as I have said and as my hon. friend from Queens knows, that can be leased if they want to experiment with building up productive beds of barren bottoms. I will tell my hon. friend, however, that you cannot get a lessee there to spend one dollar in an effort to bring back those bottoms. Hon. gentlemen opposite have always taken the ground that we were endeavouring to make political capital out of this question. On different occasions I have said that I have just as many friends on one side of this question as on the other. The barren grounds are there; if the government want to develop them we have no objection to the leasing of those grounds. If they want to try to build up productive areas there they are perfectly at liberty to do so, but when the department attempts to take the good producing areas and lease them to private individuals, that is where we step in and say something should be done on behalf of the fishermen. My hon. friend says there is no need to have anyone go down to Prince Edward Island and make an investigation because the biological station is carrying on that work now. That is not the case. They are operating under the Department of Fisheries. They may say that they operate under the biological board, but the gentleman who is there is working under the director of the Department of Fisheries, and carrying out the plans they suggest. In all fairness I say a commission should be appointed in accordance with the request of the fishermen. Let them bring in a report, and if they say that the fishermen are wrong in their contention, then I am willing to abide by their decision. If on the other hand they say that the department is leasing productive areas to private individuals, then I say that practice should be stopped, and the barren areas should be leased. Will the minister tell the committee if it is the policy of his department to continue leasing those splendid productive areas to private individuals?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
On application being
received, the policy hitherto has been to give consideration to whom the lease should be granted. It seems to me reasonable that the applicant first to be considered should be the one nearest to the area in question, next the people living behind it, and third the people

Supply-Fisheries

of the province generally. In that way the areas pass into the hands of those who can most easily and most economically work them. The hon. member should bear in mind that this work was begun and is being carried on in close cooperation with the government of Prince Edward Island, and the investigation under Doctor Needier, who is working for the biological board, is being and will be carried on. I should be glad to give careful consideration to the views expressed by the hon. member. It may be that as time goes on reconsideration should be given to the policy hitherto adopted.

I should like to call
attention to the fact that there are other oyster fishing grounds in the maritime provinces than those in Prince Edward Island. When I was a boy there was a considerable amount of oyster fishing in the three rivers running into Pictou harbour. We also had oyster fishing at Merigomish bay, Wallace, Caribou, Pugwash and Antigonish bay. However, for some reason which I am not prepared to explain, that fishing has been practically abandoned, and I should like the minister to make some investigations with regard to the waters I have named. If those waters were restocked I can see no reason why we should not again have oyster fishing as profitable as we had forty or fifty years ago. I hope the minister will be good enough to give some assurance that something will be done in this connection.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Perhaps the hon. member has forgotten that we cannot proceed in this matter except by agreement with the province. The bottoms are under the control of the provinces. In the case of Prince Edward Island cooperation resulted in these investigational works being carried out. As Nova Scotia has not come into agreement with the dominion, so far as oyster fisheries are concerned, the dominion cannot carry out such works there.
Surely the minister could ask the government of Nova Scotia to cooperate. It would not take long to do that.

The oyster fishermen of
Queens county are in accord with what the department has done in connection with oyster farming. More each year are anxious to obtain leases on the barren areas, and from time to time they request that additional surveys of harbours and bays be made. For instance, at the present time demands are being made to have surveys made of Alexandra bay, Pownal bay, Vernon river, Orwell bay

and Pinnette bay, with a view to obtaining leases. I believe last year a statement was made by an hon. member to the effect that these leases were taking away the rights of the fishermen. May I say that there is no branch of the Department of Fisheries which at the present time has such possibilities of development as has the oyster fishing branch. To-day production in Canada is very much limited; we are not able to supply the domestic demand. Oyster farming is carried on on the Atlantic and Pacific coasts, but the production last year amounted to only 24,659 barrels. This amount was made up of 8,273 barrels from New Brunswick, 10,160 from Prince Edward Island, 3,120 from British Columbia and 3,106 from Nova Scotia. That is not sufficient for the demand in Canada alone, consequently many importations were made. For the information of hon. members I shall indicate the points from which importations came. From the United States 1,094 barrels of oysters imported in the shell were valued at 86,938. From the same country 104,882 gallons of shelled oysters valued at $161,540 were imported. Again from the United States we received 106,1,17 pint cans valued at $11,145 and 4.701 quart cans valued at $1,896. Prepared or dried oysters were shipped in from China and Japan to the value of about $10,000. The total importations from outside sources were valued at $200,000.
I should like to see the department continue the development of oyster farming, and particularly the development of many of the barren areas in our bays and rivers. Some time ago the control of these bays and rivers was discussed before the privy council, and the decision was made giving the control of the waters to the federal government. Following that the federal government and the legislature of Prince Edward Island entered into a contract by which leases were granted to fishermen throughout the province. I would impress upon the acting Minister of Fisheries the necessity for further investigations, and would urge that further services be given so that our fishermen may engage in this most profitable branch of the fishing industry.

I have in my hand a petition signed by the fishermen's committee, the following names appearing:	William
McKinnon, president; Charles McFadyen, Richard Murphy, Norman Thompson, and Elisworth Gillis, secretary. I shall pass the petition on to the minister, because upon handing it to the clerk of petitions he indicated that because it asked for a grant of

Supply-Fisheries
public money it was out of order. The committee is now witness to the fact that the petition has been presented to the minister, and I trust that some action will be taken.

Following up the remarks of the hon. member for Pictou may I say that I was surprised to learn that no information had come from the government of .Nova Scotia because in correspondence with the premier of that province I gathered he was ready and willing to consider the matter of cultivating oyster beds on Bras D'Or lakes and East bay. Considerable fishing is now done at those points, and I believe the ground is fertile. I would ask the minister to give some attention to the matter, because I feel sure that Nova Scotia is ready and willing to cooperate.

The Canadian fishermen have complained that in this investigation American boats were hired and American supplies purchased, and that Canadian fishermen did not have a chance to tender or to share in the benefits so far as the money was concerned. Has this investigation 'been done absolutely by American officers on American boats?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence

Have any Canadian boats been hired?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence

Has any demand been received from fishermen in regard to the late season on the north shore of Prince Edward Island, asking that the season start on August 1 instead of August 15 as at present?

Has any decision been made with regard to these requests?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence

The matter is under consideration now?

No recommendation has

This question was under consideration two years ago-since 1932-and on one occasion it was openly stated by the present Minister of Marine (Mr. Duranleau) that the station would be established in that locality for the benefit of all fishennen in the district, and as well for the fishermen of the north shore. Now' we are g'ven to understand that it will be started as soon as possible. When I made inquiries on the first occasion the minister said that nothing had been done but that the matter was under consideration. That was the year before last, and again last year it was under consideration; this year we receive the same reply. I want to put the facts before the
[Mr. Reid 1
committee. Although the station has been promised by the federal government, through the Minister of Fisheries, and although the matter has been under consideration for some time now, the minister at that time having [DOT]ed us to believe that he was in constant mmmunication with the provincial government, there having been recommendations from them and from his officials, nothing has been done in this matter. Have any steps been taken by the biological board in the matter of research in the bay of Chaleur for the development of scallop beds in that section of the province?

Information is not being
sought by the biological board at the present time, but of course, as the hon. member will recall, investigational work has been done in the past by the department in that area, and the results of that investigation were then published.

This vote is for a very worthy purpose. Last year when it was being discussed the then acting minister promised me, in answer to a question, that he would grant a similar vote to the fishermen of British Columbia if we recommended a suitable association qualifying in the same way as this one does. Two weeks ago I presented such an application to the minister. I do not think I had a reply but I trust he will consider the matter and possibly put an item in the supplementary estimates. The association I recommended was the largest one in British Columbia, one of long existence and considerable reputation. You have only to look up Hansard to see that the minister defintely said that if we put forward a claim of that kind it would be favourably considered.

If the minister is considering grants to associations they should all be taken care of. One is not more important than another. Far be it from me to raise any sectional or constitutional cry, but the Pacific coast has been rather neglected as regards assistance to fishermen's associations. I do not need to point out any difference in importance as between British Columbia and the maritimes; one is as important as the

Supply-In tenor
other. But if grants are to be given to one, all fishermen's organizations, provided they are functioning legitimately and in good condition, should have their applications for grants favourably considered. I have in mind the fishermen's protective association on the Fraser river at two points, one above and one below the bridge. I believe the active membership is over one thousand, and I ask the minister to give consideration to that association also.
Would the minister give us some information on this point?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext: The hon. member will probably realize that in the maritimes there is one fishermen's association which can speak with one voice for the fishermen there. A practical difficulty occurs to me that on the Pacific coast there is a considerable number of fishermen's associations, and if an application came in from one of them, applications from all the rest should certainly be considered at the same time. This might add to the government's difficulties in making a decision. Of course the door is never closed to the consideration of applications that may come in, but I cannot go further than to say that consideration will be given.

Possibly the minister has answered himself. The reason why there is only one association in the maritimes is the grant given; it has amalgamated them into one and it was used for that purpose. At one time there were scores of these petty associations, and the very fact that such a grant was forthcoming and that by their coming together in one united body they could obtain it, encouraged them to cooperate. As regards any difficulty as to which society or association in British Columbia should get the grant, I do not think the minister would find us petty in that connection. I would suggest giving it for this year at any rate to the largest one, and as the one I recommended happens to be not only the largest but the oldest in that province, dating back I think some twenty years and having a good record as the deputy minister knows, I do not think any of the smaller associations would take exception to that or put up a demand to be considered at the same time. Probably this would result in the formation, as has been spoken of by the minister, of one large association for the whole province; but as the hon. member for New Westminster says, we are not being treated fairly when no recognition of that kind is being extended to British Columbia.

What is the amount of road that remains to be constructed in the national parks area to link up with the British Columbia section?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Does the hon. gentleman refer to the Big Bend road?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: On the eastern section of the road, that is the section lying between Donald and Canoe river, there are some sixteen miles to complete, including the bridge over the Canoe river. On that stretch a certain amount of work has been done comprising rock cut and a certain amount of grading, but the road from Donald to Canoe river, that is the eastern leg, has been completely graded and surfaced with the exception of some sixteen miles at the northern end. On the western leg the road has been partly completed to a distance of some fifty-eight and a half miles. It is not completed in the sense that it has all been graded and gravelled, but it is in a passable condition. There remain on that section approximately thirty-five miles which require new construction, in other words on which no work has been done.
At the present rate of progress how long will it take to complete the entire gap in the Big Bend?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The eastern leg, that is the leg for which the dominion government is responsible, could, if funds were made available, be completed this year; but the western leg, which is a responsibility of the province of British Columbia, would it is estimated take practically two years to complete, that is if all' the available crews which could advantageously be used were employed.
Are any of the construction crews, that is in the unemployment camps, being used on the British Columbia end of this particular piece of road?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, last season under the Department of National Defence certain camps were in operation on that road. There are none at the present time, I understand. The work which they were doing consisted in putting that portion of the road constructed by the province into fairly passable shape, clearing out landslides and doing a certain amount of grading. The work on the eastern leg was carried on under the Public Works Construction Act.
Could the minister give an estimate of the value of the work done by the men in the camps?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I have not the figures; that would have to be given by the Department of National Defence.

As this item includes historic sites, I take this opportunity to thank the minister for the cairn which has been erected at Cabano, in Temiscouata county, in remembrance of Vieux Chemin du Lac and Fort Ingall. May I ask the minister to see that a memorial tablet is put on that house? It is quite forgotten now, and it should be brought to the attention of passersby.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The hon. member for
